Song of Moses
SONG uv MOH-zez
noun phrase (biblical text)
From Old English sang (song, from singan, to sing) + Old English Moyses (Moses, from Hebrew Mosheh, traditionally connected to mashah, to draw out, referring to Pharaoh's daughter drawing him from the Nile, Exod 2:10). The phrase designates two distinct biblical songs attributed to Moses: the Exodus 15 triumphal song at the Red Sea, and the Deuteronomy 32 valedictory poem before Moses' death. Revelation 15:3 fuses both into an eschatological anthem of the redeemed.

Biblical Definition

The Song of Moses refers to two distinct poetic compositions attributed to Moses in the Hebrew canon. The first (Exodus 15:1–18) is the triumphal song sung by Moses and the children of Israel immediately after the crossing of the Red Sea, celebrating God's defeat of Pharaoh's army: “I will sing to the LORD, for He has triumphed gloriously!” (15:1). It is one of the oldest Hebrew poems in existence, organized around the character of YHWH as divine warrior who alone defeats the enemy of his people. The second (Deuteronomy 32:1–43) is Moses' valedictory poem delivered near the end of his life, commanded by God (Deut 31:19–22) as a testimony that Israel would forget God, suffer covenantal discipline, and ultimately be vindicated when God avenges the blood of his servants. Both songs share a common theological core: God's sovereign, saving, and judging action in history on behalf of his covenant people. Revelation 15:3 brings both songs into eschatological focus, placing the song of Moses alongside the song of the Lamb as the praise of the victorious martyred church before the throne: “Great and marvelous are Your works, O Lord God, the Almighty. Righteous and true are Your ways, O King of the nations.” The connection is typological: as Moses led Israel through the sea into the wilderness, Christ leads his church through the waters of death into the eschatological rest; as Israel sang at the far shore, the redeemed sing at the far shore of history. The psalmic tradition (especially Ps 90, attributed to Moses) extends this Mosaic prophetic-poetic voice across the canon.

Webster 1828 Definition

Two biblical songs attributed to Moses — the Red Sea triumph (Exod 15:1–18) and the Mosaic valediction (Deut 32:1–43) — united in Revelation 15:3 as the eschatological praise of the redeemed church, whose victory over the beast is typologically continuous with Israel's deliverance from Egypt.

SONG OF MOSES, n. Either of two major poetic compositions attributed to Moses: (1) the Exodus 15 Red Sea triumph; (2) the Deuteronomy 32 covenantal valediction.

2. EXODUS 15 (the Song of the Sea, Shirat HaYam): sung by Moses and Israel at the far shore after the destruction of Pharaoh's army — the oldest datable poetry in the Old Testament, structured around the divine warrior theology of YHWH as the sole defeater of his people's enemy.

3. DEUTERONOMY 32 (the Great Song): a prophetic valediction commanded by God (Deut 31:19–22) to be taught to Israel as a witness against their future rebellion; predicts apostasy, covenantal discipline, and ultimate vindication through God's jealousy for his own name and his servants' blood.

4. REVELATION 15:3 (the eschatological fusion): the martyred victors standing on the sea of glass sing “the song of Moses, the bondservant of God, and the song of the Lamb” — the great Exodus song becomes the template for the final triumph of the church over the beast.

5. TYPOLOGICAL CHAIN: Red Sea crossing (Exod 14–15) → baptism into Moses (1 Cor 10:2) → baptism into Christ (Rom 6:3–5) → the sea of glass (Rev 4:6; 15:2) → the eternal triumph song (Rev 15:3–4): the same pattern of deliverance-through-water-into-freedom, ascending through the ages.

Key Scripture

Exod 15:1 — "Then sang Moses and the children of Israel this song unto the LORD, and spake, saying, I will sing unto the LORD, for he hath triumphed gloriously: the horse and his rider hath he thrown into the sea."

Exod 15:2 — "The LORD is my strength and song, and he is become my salvation: he is my God, and I will prepare him an habitation; my father's God, and I will exalt him."

Deut 32:3 — "Because I will publish the name of the LORD: ascribe ye greatness unto our God."

Rev 15:3 — "And they sing the song of Moses the servant of God, and the song of the Lamb, saying, Great and marvellous are thy works, Lord God Almighty; just and true are thy ways, thou King of saints."

Modern Corruption

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The Song of Moses has not been a major site of ideological contest, though critical scholarship has dated portions of Exodus 15 very late to undermine its Mosaic authenticity, and Deuteronomy 32 has been subjected to historical-critical partition into multiple sources.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principal challenge to the Song of Moses comes not from progressive cultural appropriation but from the documentary hypothesis tradition in biblical criticism, which denies Mosaic authorship of Exodus 15 and Deuteronomy 32 on the grounds of linguistic anachronisms and stylistic arguments. The Reformed and conservative evangelical response notes that the archaizing features of Exod 15 are characteristic of the oldest Semitic poetry (Cross, Freedman), that the Deuteronomistic language of Deut 32 is consistent with a late-Mosaic date, and that Jesus himself attests both Mosaic authorship and the theological integrity of the Pentateuch as a whole (John 5:46).

The principle to recover from the Song of Moses is the theology of triumphant praise grounded in historical redemption. The Israelites did not sing before the crossing but after it — the song arose from the accomplished fact of deliverance, not from aspirational hope alone. This is the pattern of Christian doxology: the foundation of praise is the finished work of Christ, the accomplished redemption at Calvary and the empty tomb, which generates the “new song” the Revelation apostrophe envisions (Rev 5:9; 15:3). Praise is not worked up by technique; it breaks out from the knowledge of what God has done.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The Song of Moses belongs to the genre of ancient Near Eastern victory hymns, but transformed by Yahwistic theology: the warrior is not a human king but YHWH himself, the victory is purely divine, and the song's purpose is to declare God's character and name, not human heroism.

Hebrew shirah — song, singing; the feminine form of shir, used for the major biblical poems (Exod 15:1 calls it “this shirah”); the Hebrew poetic tradition has a high register distinct from prose narrative

Hebrew Shirat HaYam — the Song of the Sea; the rabbinic designation for Exodus 15, one of the most sacred texts in Jewish liturgy, sung as part of the daily morning prayers

Divine-warrior motif: YHWH as the warrior who fights for his people without human military contribution — the horse and rider are cast into the sea by God alone (Exod 15:1,21); the Israelites were silent witnesses of deliverance, not active fighters

Deuteronomy 32's covenant-lawsuit pattern (rib): the song calls heaven and earth as witnesses to God's righteousness and Israel's rebellion, a forensic structure found throughout the prophets (Isa 1:2; Mic 6:1–2) and rooted in the Mosaic covenant

Revelation 15:3 typological fusion: the martyred victors sing both Moses' song and the Lamb's song as one, because the one redemption-pattern (deliverance through death into new life) underlies both Exodus and Cross

Usage

"Paul's typological use of the Red Sea crossing in 1 Corinthians 10:1–4 — “all were baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea” — establishes the Exodus pattern as the template for Christian baptismal theology: passage through water as the death and resurrection of Christ applied to the believer."

"Miriam's response in Exodus 15:20–21 — leading the women with tambourines in antiphonal singing — establishes the pattern of corporate sung worship as a response to God's saving acts: the earliest description of congregational music in the Bible is worship arising from redemption."

"The Jewish Passover Seder includes the recitation of Exodus 15 as part of the Hallel (praise) section, connecting every generation's Passover celebration to the original Exodus event and its inaugural song — a liturgical pattern the church inherits in its own Passover, the Lord's Supper."
